title: System Design Interview Question: Design URL Shortener
partialText:
This is a system design interview question, which is to design a URL shortener tool like TinyURL or Bitly from the ground up. We’ll cover everything from design requirements, architecture, and component design to scaling for high-performance and security best practices.

Defining the Scope: Functional and Non-functional Requirements

First, we need to define this system’s functional and non-functional requirements.

We have two functional requirements:

  1. When given a long URL, we have to create a short URL
  2. When given a short URL, we must redirect the user to the long URL.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

The non-functional requirements for our service are to prioritize low latency (fast responses) and high availability (always online).

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Clarifying Questions for the Interviewer

Here are some clarifying questions that we might ask the interviewer to ensure we’re aligned on the system’s scale:

  • Usage: Estimate the number of URLs we’ll need to create each second (let’s say it’s 1000).
  • Characters: Can we use numbers and letters (alphanumeric) or other symbols? (We’ll assume alphanumeric characters).
  • Uniqueness: Do we generate a unique short URL each time, even if multiple users submit the same long URL? (For this design, we will).

Estimation: Data Math

With this information, we need to calculate how long the URL should be after shortening. Of course, we’re trying to make it as short as possible, but we need to keep in mind the number of created URLs each year.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

First, let’s estimate the number of unique URLs needed for a significant period. A common approach is to plan for at least a few years of operation. For simplicity, let’s calculate for 10 years.

  • Seconds in a Year: Seconds in a year: 60 seconds/minute × 60 minutes/hour × 24 hours/day × 365 days/year = 31.536 million seconds
  • Total Seconds in 10 Years: 31.536 million × 10= 315.36 million seconds
  • Total URLs in 10 Years: 1,000 × 315.36 million = 315.36 billion unique URLs

This means our database will handle 1000 writes per second and every year, we will have 1000 × 60 × 60 × 24 × 365 = 31.5B URLs created. If we assume that we will typically have 10x more reads than writes, that means that we’ll be getting more than 10 × 1000 = 10000 reads per second.

Now, we need to figure out how many characters will give us enough unique short URLs for our 10-year volume. Given that the character set size is 62, the length of the URL identifier can be calculated as follows:

  • 6²¹ = 62 unique URLs (1 character)
  • 6²² = 3844 unique URLs (2 characters)
  • …and so on.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Continuing this calculation, we see that 6²⁷ (around 3.5 trillion) is the first value larger than our projected 315 billion URLs needed.

Therefore, to support our projected growth over the next ten years, our shortened URLs need a minimum of 7 characters.

High-Level Architecture

Our system will have these key components:

Users: We will have users who send their long URLs to be shortened or who send us a short URL, and we need to redirect them to the long URL.

Load Balancer: All of these requests go through a load balancer, which distributes the traffic across multiple web server instances to ensure high availability and balance of the load.

Web Servers: These server replicas are responsible for handling the incoming HTTP requests.

URL Shortener Service: We also need a URL shortener service that contains the core logic for generating short URLs, storing URL mappings, and retrieving the original URLs for redirection.

Database: Stores the connection between short URLs and their long counterparts. Before designing the database, we need to consider the potential storage requirements for our shortened URLs.

Each URL will include the unique identifier (roughly 7 bytes), the long URL (up to 100 bytes), and user metadata (estimated at 500 bytes). This means we need up to 1000 bytes per URL. Over ten years, with our projected volume, this translates to approximately 315 terabytes of data.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Before moving any further, let’s first think about the API Design of our single web server.

API Design

Let’s define the basic API operations for our service. As stated in our functional requirements, we will use a REST API, and we need two endpoints.

1. Create a Short URL (POST /urls)

Input: JSON payload containing the long URL {“longUrl”: “https://example.com/very-long-url"}

Output: JSON payload with the shortened URL {“shortUrl”: “https://tiny.url/3ad32p9"} and 201 Created status code.

If the request is invalid or malformed, we’ll return 400 Bad Request response, and in case the requested URL already exists in the system, we'll respond with 409 Conflict.

2. Redirect to Long URL (GET /urls/{shortUrlId})

Input: shortUrlId path parameter

Output: Response with 301 Moved Permanently and the newly created short URL in the response body as JSON { "shortUrl": "https://tiny.url/3ad32p9" }

Press enter or click to view image in full size

301 status code instructs the browser to cache the information, which means that the next time the user types in the short URL, the browser will automatically redirect to the long URL without reaching the server.

However, if you want to track each request’s analytics and ensure it goes through your system, use the 302 status code instead.

Database: Storing the shortened URLs

The next part is the Database layer. This layer stores the mapping between short URLs and long URLs. It should be optimized for fast read and write operations.

The schema could be simple: a primary key for the short URL id and fields for the long URL and possibly creation metadata.

{
  "shortUrlId": "3ad32p9",
  "longUrl": "https://example.com/very-long-url",
  "creationDate": "2024-03-08T12:00:00Z",
  "userId": "user123",
  "clicks": 1023,
  "metadata": {
    "title": "Example Web Page",
    "tags": ["example", "web", "url shortener"],
    "expireDate": "2025-03-08T12:00:00Z"
  },
  "isActive": true
}

Here, we mostly need to think about the reads we will get to the database. If we typically get 1000 Writes per second, then we can assume that we at least get 10–100.000 Reads per second.

In this case, we need to use a high-performance database that supports fast reads and writes. That means we need to go with a NoSQL database (like a document store like MongoDB, a wide-column store like Cassandra, or a key-value store like DynamoDB) since they’re specifically designed to handle a large amount of scale.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

It won’t be ACID compliant, but we are not concerned about it because we’re not going to do a bunch of JOINs or complex queries, and we don’t need those ACID rules and atomic transactions here.

URL Shortener Service

One of the core parts of this system is the URL Shortener Service. This service generates short URLs without introducing collisions between different long URLs pointing to the same short URL.

There are various methods to implement this service; here are some of them:

  • Hashing: Generate a hash of the long URL and use a part of it as the identifier. However, hashing can lead to collisions.
  • Auto-increment IDs: Use a database auto-increment ID and encode it to a short string. This ensures uniqueness but might be predictable.
  • Custom Algorithm: Design a custom algorithm to generate unique IDs with a mix of characters to ensure uniqueness and non-predictability.

For example, to avoid collisions, there’s a very simple way — we can generate all the possible keys with 7 characters and store them in a database as keys, where the key is the generated URL and the value is boolean; if it’s true, then this URL is already used, and if it’s false, then we can use this URL to create a new map.

So, whenever a user requests to generate a key, we can find a URL from this database that is not currently in use and map it to the long URL in the request body.

Do you think we will use an SQL or NoSQL database in this case? Consider a scenario where two users asked to shorten their long URLs, and they both got mapped to the same key from this database.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

In this case, the URL will be mapped to one of their requests, and the other one will be broken. So, we will use SQL because it comes with ACID properties. We can create a transaction for each session here to perform these steps in isolation, and we won’t have such issues in this case.

High Availability & Low Latency

Our current system obviously won’t be able to handle 1000 URLs per second of traffic.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Caching

To make this more scalable, we first need a Caching layer (e.g., Redis) to cache popular URLs for quick retrieval in an in-memory cache with tools like Redis.

Given that some URLs might be accessed much more frequently than others, we need an eviction policy that prioritizes frequently accessed items. Two suitable caching eviction policies for this scenario are:

  • The LRU eviction policy removes the least recently accessed items first. This policy is effective for a URL shortener because it ensures that the cache keeps the most recently and frequently accessed URLs available, which can significantly reduce access times for popular links.
  • Or a Time To Live TTL-based eviction policy assigns a fixed time-to-live to each cache entry. Once an entry’s TTL expires, it is removed from the cache. This policy can be useful for URL shortening services to handle the caching of URLs that are only popular for a short duration.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

TTL can also help us automatically refresh the cache contents and can be combined with other policies like LRU for more effective cache management.

Database Scaling: Combining Replication and Sharding

We need to implement replication and sharding strategies to ensure that the database supports high availability, fault tolerance, and scalability.

Considering that our 7-character set has 3.5T unique URLs, we can use key-based sharding to distribute the URL records evenly across multiple shards.

Let’s say we distribute it across 3 shards, and each shard will store approximately 1.16T URLs. This ensures scalability as the number of URLs grows.

We can also implement master-slave replication within each shard to ensure high availability and fault tolerance. This setup allows for quick failover and recovery in case of node failures.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Optionally, if the service targets a global user base, we can consider geographical sharding and replication to minimize latency and improve user experience across different regions.

This combination allows the service to handle a large volume of URL shortenings and redirections with minimal downtime and fast response times.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Security Considerations

Here are some security considerations to keep in mind for our service:

  • Input Validation: Let’s sanitize every URL a user submits. We must check for valid protocols (HTTP, HTTPS, etc.) and ensure the URL is well-formed. This helps prevent injection attacks.
  • Rate Limiting: We can protect our service from DDoS attacks by limiting the number of requests a single source can make. Consider a token bucket algorithm for this.
  • Monitoring and Logging: A robust logging system (like the ELK stack) is essential. It lets us analyze logs to find bottlenecks and suspicious activity and ensure overall system health.
  • Obfuscation: We don’t want easily predicted short URLs. To deter attackers from guessing valid links, let’s add randomness to our generation algorithm.
  • Link Expiration: Optionally, we can consider allowing users to set expiration dates on their shortened URLs. This limits the lifespan of potentially malicious links.

If you’d like to learn more about each component we discussed here, I have a detailed System Design Interview Concepts Tutorial that goes over each one in more detail.

System Design Interview Question: Design URL Shortener was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Generative AI Design Patterns: All-In-One Page
partialText:
Patterns to Move Beyond Simple Prompts To Production-Ready GenAI Applications.

I’ve spent a few weeks going through Valliappa Lakshmanan and Hannes Hapke’s book Generative AI Design Patterns, mostly because I kept running into the same wall while working on our GenAI discovery platform. There were times when I applied solutions, but couldn’t confidently say why it would work, or whether it was the right fix versus one that happened to work this time. The book names 32 of these fixes and reading through it felt less like learning something new and more like finally getting labels for things I’d been doing by feel for many months — and a few things I hadn’t tried yet that explained gaps I couldn’t place.

I previously wrote detailed blog posts describing all the patterns, and this post is a summary of them. This can be used as a reference to know what patterns exist and what problem they solve.

Part 1 — The AI Output Problem Nobody Talks About — It’s Not the Model

Part 2 — The AI Hallucination Problem Nobody Talks About — It’s Not the Model. Grounding & Retrieval

Part 3 — The AI Quality Problem Nobody Talks About — Your System Is Flying Blind. Evaluation & Self-Improvement

Part 4 — The AI Agent Problem Nobody Talks About — Intelligence Is Not Architecture. Orchestration & Agents

I am sure you might have used most of these but would have never known the name of most of them. This post should help you familiarize yourself with all.

1. Controlling Content Style

Controlling Content Style is the category of patterns that shape how a model writes — tone, format, and compliance with rules — rather than what it knows: Logits Masking, Grammar, Style Transfer, Reverse Neutralization, and Content Optimization.

Logits Masking

Remove banned tokens at sampling time so forbidden words can’t appear.

Problem: You need certain words or phrases to never show up in the output — for legal, brand, or compliance reasons — and a prompt instruction like “don’t mention competitors” is a request, not a guarantee.

How it solves it: Intercept generation at the token level. Before the model samples its next word, zero out the probability of anything on the banned list, then renormalize what’s left and sample from that.

Say your support bot must never mention a competitor’s product by name. Instead of hoping the system prompt holds under pressure, you mask those tokens at the sampling stage — the model cannot produce them, no matter how the conversation is steered.

Trade off: Be aware too aggressive masking can produce stilted or incoherent text, since it removes options mid-generation rather than steering the model’s intent.

Grammar

Enforce structured outputs via a formal schema to ensure 100% reliable parsing.

Problem: Downstream code needs the output to conform to a strict format — valid JSON, a specific schema — and “usually correct” breaks a pipeline the moment it isn’t.

How it solves it: Constrain token generation against a formal grammar or schema (BNF, JSON schema) so the model can only ever produce tokens that keep the output structurally valid.

I hit this constantly extracting structured metadata from well completion reports — dates, coordinates, formation names — where a malformed field silently breaks the loader downstream. Constraining generation to the schema means invalid output simply can’t happen, instead of catching it after the fact.

Trade-off: A rigid schema can force a bad-fit answer when the real data doesn’t cleanly match the shape you defined.

Style Transfer

Use few-shot examples to demonstrate the target style instead of describing it textually.

Problem: You know the tone you want, but writing rules for it doesn’t work — tone resists being reduced to a checklist.

How it solves it: Show the model examples of the target style instead of describing it. Few-shot examples or light fine-tuning teach the conversion better than any style guide.

Converting a dense technical spec into a blog-post-ready explanation is a style transfer problem. Ten good examples of “spec paragraph in, readable paragraph out” beat two pages of tone guidelines every time.

Trade-off: Quality depends entirely on how good and representative your examples are — weak or biased examples propagate straight into the output.

Reverse Neutralization:

Decouple generation and styling by producing neutral content first, then applying a fine-tuned restyling layer.

Problem: You want output in a specific style, but you only have finished examples of that style — no clean way to generate the neutral content that would normally precede the stylizing step.

How it solves it: Generate a plain, neutral draft first with a general-purpose model, then pass it through a second model fine-tuned specifically to convert neutral text into the target style.

Region-specific legal correspondence is the textbook — the underlying content (what needs to be communicated) is straightforward, but local phrasing conventions are a specialized skill that a general model won’t get right on its own.

Trade-off: Two model calls instead of one adds latency and cost, and errors in the neutral draft carry through to the styled output.

Content Optimization

Implement a feedback loop by scoring generated variants against each other and optimizing parameters toward the highest-rated outputs.

Problem: You don’t know which stylistic choices actually move the needle, and testing them one by one by hand isn’t realistic at any real volume.

How it solves it: Generate paired content variants, score them against each other with an evaluator, build a preference dataset from the comparisons, and tune on that.

Ad copy is the classic use case — you’re not sure if shorter headlines or specific numbers move the needle, so instead of arguing about it, you generate pairs, let an evaluator pick winners, and tune toward what the data actually shows.

Trade-off: Needs a reliable evaluator and real volume to build a meaningful preference dataset — a noisy evaluator just produces noisy tuning.

2. Adding Knowledge

Patterns that ground the model in external, current, or private information instead of relying on what it memorized during training.

Basic RAG

Ground generation by injecting retrieved context into the prompt at inference time.

Problem: The model’s training data is stale, or it just doesn’t include the private documents you need answers about, so it either doesn’t know or makes something up.

How it solves it: Retrieve relevant text from a knowledge base and inject it into the prompt before the model answers.

This is where everyone starts — Ask a policy question, retrieve the three most relevant paragraphs from the actual policy document and hand both to the model. It’s also the pattern everyone eventually discovers isn’t enough on its own.

Trade-off: Answer quality is capped by retrieval quality — a strong model paired with weak retrieval still gives weak answers.

Semantic Indexing

Retrieve by embedding similarity instead of keyword overlap.

Problem: Keyword search fails the moment the user’s words don’t match the document’s words, and it fails completely once you’ve got tables and images mixed in with text.

How it solves it: Embed text, tables, and images into the same vector space, then find matches by comparing meaning rather than exact wording.

A query like “how do I cancel” and a document titled “termination procedure” share zero words but the same meaning — semantic indexing is what lets the retriever connect them anyway.

Trade-off: Embeddings can conflate similar-sounding but distinct concepts, and reindexing a large corpus isn’t cheap.

Indexing at Scale

Filter and rerank retrieval candidates using metadata to prevent outdated or conflicting sources from surfacing.

Problem: Your knowledge base has three versions of the same policy floating around, and the retriever will confidently pull the wrong one.

How it solves it: Tag chunks with metadata — effective date, region, product version — and filter by that metadata before retrieval, then rerank what’s left.

In a subsurface knowledge base with revised well reports, filtering to “current revision only” before the similarity search runs is the difference between a right answer and a confidently wrong one.

Trade-off: Over-filtering on metadata can exclude a genuinely relevant older document that the filter treats as simply outdated.

Index-aware Retrieval

Search using a hypothetical answer’s embedding to close the gap between question phrasing and document phrasing.

Problem: The user’s actual question almost never appears in your documents word for word — they use different terms, jargon, or phrasing than whatever’s in the source text.

How it solves it: Generate a hypothetical answer to the question first, then search using that hypothetical answer’s embedding instead of the raw question.

It sounds backward until you watch it fix a retrieval miss; nothing else explains — searching with a plausible answer instead of the bare question surfaces chunks a literal query would have skipped entirely.

Trade-off: The hypothetical answer can itself be wrong, and searching against a wrong guess sometimes pulls in worse chunks than the plain question would have.

Node Postprocessing

Rerank retrieved chunks with a cross-encoder before they reach the prompt.

Problem: A first-pass retriever ranks by broad topical similarity, so the chunks it surfaces can all be “about” the right subject while still missing the one specific detail the question actually needs.

How it solves it: Run a reranker — usually a cross-encoder — over the retrieved chunks before they reach the prompt, so a fast first-pass retriever gets a second, more careful pass on top.

I’ve seen this fix cases where the “correct” chunk sat at position four out of five — reachable by the retriever, but never getting into the prompt until reranking put it first.

Trade-off: Reranking adds a second inference pass — a latency cost that’s fine for a chatbot and expensive for high-throughput batch work.

Trustworthy Generation

Attach citations and route low-confidence outputs to human review to preserve user trust.

Problem: The system will be wrong sometimes — that’s unavoidable — and users need a way to tell when to trust an answer and when not to.

How it solves it: Add citations so people can check sources, detect out-of-domain questions, and route low-confidence answers to a human instead of shipping them with the same tone of confidence as everything else.

A confident wrong answer does more damage than an honest “I’m not sure, let me check.” Routing low-confidence responses to review keeps the failure mode visible instead of hidden.

Trade-off: Routing too conservatively to human review quietly erodes the automation gains the system was built for in the first place.

Deep Search

Iterate search, read, and reasoning cycles to resolve multi-hop queries.

Problem: Some questions need connecting facts across three or four separate documents, and a single retrieval pass just isn’t built for that.

How it solves it: Loop through search, read, and reason repeatedly — decide if you have enough to answer, and if not, search again with a refined query.

Multi-hop questions like “which of these reports contradicts the completion date in the other one” need this loop. Single-pass RAG retrieves one relevant document and stop there, missing the contradiction entirely.

Trade-off: Each additional search-read-reason cycle multiplies latency and cost, making it a poor fit for anything that needs a fast response.

3. Extending Model Capabilities

Patterns that push a model’s reasoning or specialization further — changing how it thinks through a problem, or how cheaply it can be adapted to a new one.

Chain of Thought

Prompt the model to externalize intermediate reasoning before producing a final answer.

Problem: On anything requiring more than one logical step, models often jump straight to an answer — and it’s often wrong.

How it solves it: Prompt the model to reason through intermediate steps before committing to a final answer.

Still underused more than it should be — plenty of production prompts ask for “the answer” directly on tasks that genuinely need the reasoning trace to get there reliably.

Trade-off: Longer reasoning traces cost more tokens and time, and a flawed intermediate step can still lead confidently to a wrong final answer.

Tree of Thoughts

Explore and evaluate multiple reasoning branches, backtracking from unproductive paths.

Problem: Some problems don’t have a single reasoning path worth following — they have several plausible ones, and a purely linear approach commits too early.

How it solves it: Generate multiple candidate reasoning paths, evaluate each one, and expand the best while backtracking from dead ends.

Worth the extra inference cost on genuinely hard planning tasks — a strategic decision with several defensible options — and overkill on anything where one straightforward path clearly works.

Trade-off: Cost scales with how many branches get explored, so it’s expensive overhead on problems where a single straight path would have worked fine.

Adapter Tuning

Train lightweight add-on layers on a frozen base model to specialize it cheaply.

Problem: Fully fine-tuning a large model for one narrow task is expensive, and you probably don’t have the data volume to justify it anyway.

How it solves it: Train small adapter layers on top of a frozen base model — the base weights never move, only the lightweight add-on does.

A LoRA adapter trained on a few thousand support tickets gives you a specialized classifier without touching the base model at all — cheap enough to iterate on and cheap enough to throw away if it doesn’t work.

Trade-off: An adapter is only as good as its training data’s coverage — it won’t generalize past what it actually saw during training.

Evol-Instruct

Iteratively evolve a small seed instruction set into a large, difficulty-varied training dataset.

Problem: You need a large instruction-tuning dataset for a domain nobody’s built one for, and hand-writing thousands of examples isn’t realistic.

How it solves it: Seed a modest set of handwritten examples, then have an LLM iteratively evolve harder variants until the dataset has real range.

Fifty seed examples of domain-specific instructions can grow into thousands of increasingly difficult variants this way — useful the moment your task is specific enough that no public dataset covers it.

Trade-off: Evolved instructions can drift from what a real user would actually ask, so the dataset needs periodic human spot-checking.

4. Improving Reliability

Patterns that measure, correct, and stabilize LLM behavior so quality doesn’t drift silently once something ships.

LLM-as-Judge

Score open-ended model outputs against a rubric using a second model as evaluator.

Problem: GenAI output is open-ended, so there’s no fixed answer key to grade it against.

How it solves it: Score outputs against a rubric using a judge model, and track that score as the real signal instead of relying on gut feel.

Comparing two prompt versions on a hundred held-out examples with a judge model gives you a number to argue about — a lot more useful than two people disagreeing about which output “feels” better.

Trade-off: The judge model carries its own biases and blind spots, so its scores need periodic validation against actual human judgment.

Reflection

Feed a model’s own output back with critique instructions to produce a corrected second pass.

Problem: The first draft is wrong, and there’s no human sitting there to catch it before it ships.

How it solves it: Feed the model its own output back, along with instructions to check it against the source material, and let the second pass fix what the first missed.

This catches more factual-grounding errors than I expected the first time I tried it — asking the model to “check the above against the source and correct any errors” surfaces mistakes it wouldn’t flag on its own.

Trade-off: Doubles inference cost for every response, and a model can also confidently “correct” something that wasn’t wrong to begin with.

Dependency Injection

Make each step of an LLM pipeline swappable with a mock for isolated testing.

Problem: Testing one step of an LLM chain shouldn’t require running the entire chain, but that’s exactly what happens if every step is hard-wired to the next.

How it solves it: Design the chain so any step — retrieval, a tool call, another model — can be swapped for a mock during testing.

Testing a generation step against a fixed set of mock chunks instead of live retrieval means the test runs in milliseconds and doesn’t depend on the vector database being up.

Trade-off: A mocked test can keep passing while the real integration silently breaks, so this doesn’t replace integration testing.

Prompt Optimization

Systematically tune prompt wording against a held-out example set instead of by hand.

Problem: A model provider ships a new version, and the prompt you tuned carefully six months ago quietly stops working.

How it solves it: Instead of hand-editing wording every time this happens, re-optimize the prompt systematically against a held-out set of examples.

Treats prompt maintenance as an engineering problem with a measurable target, rather than a guessing game every time a vendor pushes a model update.

Trade-off: Optimizing tightly to one example set risks overfitting to it, at the cost of performance on cases outside that set.

5. Enabling Agents to Take Action

Patterns that let a model act on the world — calling tools, running code, coordinating with other agents — instead of only describing what someone else should do.

Tool Calling

Let the model emit structured function calls that a client executes and returns results from.

Problem: The model needs to actually do something — check a database, hit an API — not just describe what someone else should do.

How it solves it: The model emits a structured function call with parameters; your code executes it and returns the result for the model to use in its response.

This is the backbone of every agent that does more than chat — an assistant that can actually check inventory or place an order, instead of one that can only describe how you’d go check.

Trade-off: Every tool is a new failure surface — wrong parameters, timeouts, or an unavailable service all need to be handled explicitly.

Code Execution

Have the model generate code and run it externally instead of reasoning to an answer in text.

Problem: Some tasks are genuinely easier to solve with code than to reason through in natural language — a calculation, a data transformation.

How it solves it: Let the model write a short script and run it in an external execution engine, rather than trying to “think” its way to a numeric answer.

Asking a model to compute a statistic by reasoning about it in text is unreliable. Instead it is better to ask it to write three lines of pandas and run them.

Trade-off: Running model-generated code means sandboxing it properly; skipping that step is a real security risk.

Multi-agent Collaboration

Decompose a task across specialized, coordinating agents instead of one generalist.

Problem: One agent trying to hold every tool, every piece of context, and every step of a complex task at once starts dropping things.

How it solves it: Split the work — one plans, one retrieves, one validates — coordinated like a small team, rather than one overloaded generalist.

A research assistant built this way delegates retrieval to a specialist agent and fact-checking to another, then reconciles what comes back — instead of one agent trying to do all three jobs itself and losing track halfway through.

Trade-off: More agents means more coordination overhead, more latency, and more places for a handoff between agents to quietly go wrong.

6. Addressing Constraints

Patterns that keep cost, latency, and infrastructure under control once a system is carrying production traffic.

Small Language Model

Route simpler requests to a smaller, distilled model to cut cost and latency.

Problem: The frontier model is overkill for most of what you’re actually asking it, and you’re paying frontier prices for all of it anyway.

How it solves it: Route simple, narrow tasks to a smaller distilled model and reserve the expensive one for cases that genuinely need it.

Basic intent classification doesn’t need a large model. Routing that traffic to a distilled 3B model and reserving the large model for the genuinely ambiguous cases cuts cost without touching quality where it matters.

Trade-off: The router itself can misclassify a complex request as simple, silently degrading quality on exactly the cases that needed the larger model.

Prompt Caching

Reuse cached responses for semantically similar prompts to avoid redundant inference.

Problem: The same or near-identical prompts keep hitting the model, and you keep paying to recompute the same answer.

How it solves it: Cache responses keyed on semantic similarity, not just exact string match, so near-duplicate prompts hit the cache too.

A support system fielding the same handful of questions phrased ten different ways benefits enormously from a semantic cache — an exact-match cache would miss almost all of those near-duplicates.

Trade-off: A semantic cache can return a stale or subtly wrong answer for a prompt that only resembles a previous one, not actually matches it.

Inference Optimization

Apply continuous batching and speculative decoding to maximize GPU throughput.

Problem: Self-hosted serving is GPU-bound, and idle cycles between requests burn money for no reason.

How it solves it: Continuous batching pulls new requests into idle GPU slots as soon as they open, and speculative decoding lets a small model draft while a large model verifies.

The difference between processing requests one batch at a time with gaps, versus keeping the GPU continuously fed, shows up directly in your hosting bill at any real scale.

Trade-off: These techniques add real engineering and operational complexity — not worth taking on below a certain traffic volume.

Degradation Testing

Track TTFT, latency, and tokens-per-second against a baseline to catch quality drift early

Problem: Your uptime dashboard is green and users are still complaining the app feels slow — “up” and “fast enough” are different questions.

How it solves it: Track time-to-first-token, end-to-end latency, and tokens-per-second as first-class metrics against a baseline, and flag when they drift.

A standard health check won’t catch a model that’s technically responding but has gotten noticeably slower — these metrics will, well before users start complaining.

Trade-off: Meaningful baselines need real traffic data to establish, so the payoff shows up later in a system’s life more than on day one.

Long-Term Memory

Store and retrieve only the relevant memory slice instead of replaying full conversation history.

Problem: Replaying the entire conversation history on every prompt gets expensive fast, and eventually it won’t fit in the context window anyway. How it solves it: Store memory separately — working memory for the current task, episodic memory for past sessions — and retrieve only the slice relevant to the current turn.

A customer support assistant that’s been in a conversation for forty turns doesn’t need all forty replayed on every call — retrieving just the relevant memory slice and combining it with the current turn keeps cost flat instead of growing with every exchange.

Trade-off: Retrieval-based memory can miss or misretrieve a relevant past detail — unlike a full transcript, which never forgets anything.

7. Setting Safeguards

Patterns that reduce risk before generated content ever reaches a real user.

Template Generation

Fill pre-approved, human-reviewed templates deterministically instead of generating freely.

Problem: Sending fully generated content straight to customers is too risky, but human review of every single message doesn’t scale.

How it solves it: Pre-write and approve a set of templates; at runtime, generation does nothing riskier than filling in the blanks with deterministic substitution.

Personalized billing notifications are a good fit — the structure and legal language get reviewed once, and only the specific numbers change per customer at send time.

Trade-off: Every genuinely novel situation the templates don’t cover falls back to either a poor-fit template or manual handling.

Assembled Reformat

Separate low-risk data assembly from generation so formatting never invents facts.

Problem: Content needs to look polished, but generating it dynamically risks factual drift creeping into numbers or specifics that shouldn’t move. How it solves it: Split the job in two — assemble the underlying data with simple, low-risk logic first, then use generation only to format it, never to invent any part of it.

A product catalog page is a clean example — prices and specs get assembled from verified data, and generation is only responsible for arranging that data attractively, never for supplying it.

Trade-off: Limits the system to what the assembly logic already anticipated — it can’t handle content that genuinely needs judgment.

Self-Check

Flag low-probability token spans as likely hallucinations using the model’s own output probabilities.

Problem: You want to catch hallucinations cheaply, without the cost of a second model call just to verify the first one.

How it solves it: Look at the token-level probabilities of the original response — unusually low-confidence sequences are a decent, nearly free signal that something’s off.

Works well as a cheap first filter for factual (not creative) responses — flag the low-confidence spans for a closer look instead of accepting or rejecting the whole response.

Trade-off: Low token probability doesn’t always mean wrong, and high probability doesn’t always mean right — it’s just a signal.

Guardrails

Wrap every LLM call with pre- and post-processing checks for injection, PII, and policy violations.

Problem: The moment an application is exposed to real users, it’s exposed to people actively trying to break it. How it solves it: Wrap every LLM call with pre-processing (prompt injection, PII detection) and post-processing (moderation, policy checks) — and extend the same wrapping to any tool or retrieval step the model touches.

Treat this as infrastructure from day one, not something bolted on right before launch — the cost of adding it after an incident is always higher than the cost of building it in.

Trade-off: Aggressive guardrails create false positives that block legitimate requests, and every added check adds latency to the pipeline.

That’s all 32. None of them live in isolation in a real system — a RAG pipeline that survives contact with actual users is usually Basic RAG plus Semantic Indexing plus Node Postprocessing plus Trustworthy Generation running together, at minimum. That’s also why “we added RAG” and “our RAG system actually works” turn out to mean such different things in practice.

I’ll probably come back to a few of these — Long-Term Memory and Multi-agent Collaboration especially — with their own deep dives once I’ve pushed them further in my projects. For now, this is the map I wanted on hand.

title: Running ONNX GenAI Model on GPU — How to Set Up Driver, CUDA 13, cuDNN, and NuGet
partialText:
Background

In my previous two articles, I walked through edge AI development on the .NET stack using the ONNX model format. Those posts relied on CPU hardware. In this article, I will extend that path and use a GPU for GenAI inference. If you want to know how much faster inference can get on GPU — or how to set up a local CUDA environment on Windows — this post is for you. Let’s get started.

Model

As I mentioned in the first article in this series, the Phi-3-Mini-4K-Instruct-onnx model ships in several variants for different compute targets: cuda, directml, and cpu_and_mobile.

In that earlier post we used the cpu_and_mobile build. Today we switch to the cuda folder. We still use a quantized model; the weight file is about 2.3 GB.

The model’s genai_config.json makes the execution provider explicit—provider_options is set to CUDA:

{
    "model": {
        "bos_token_id": 1,
        "context_length": 4096,
        "decoder": {
            "session_options": {
                "log_id": "onnxruntime-genai",
                "provider_options": [
                    {
                        "cuda": {
                            "enable_cuda_graph": "0"
                        }
                    }
                ]
            },
            "filename": "phi3-mini-4k-instruct-cuda-int4-rtn-block-32.onnx",
            "head_size": 96,
            "hidden_size": 3072,
            "inputs": {
                "input_ids": "input_ids",
                "attention_mask": "attention_mask",
                "past_key_names": "past_key_values.%d.key",
                "past_value_names": "past_key_values.%d.value"
            },
            "outputs": {
                "logits": "logits",
                "present_key_names": "present.%d.key",
                "present_value_names": "present.%d.value"
            },
            "num_attention_heads": 32,
            "num_hidden_layers": 32,
            "num_key_value_heads": 32
        },
        "eos_token_id": [
            32000,
            32001,
            32007
        ],
        "pad_token_id": 32000,
        "type": "phi3",
        "vocab_size": 32064
    },
    "search": {
        "diversity_penalty": 0.0,
        "do_sample": false,
        "early_stopping": true,
        "length_penalty": 1.0,
        "max_length": 4096,
        "min_length": 0,
        "no_repeat_ngram_size": 0,
        "num_beams": 1,
        "num_return_sequences": 1,
        "past_present_share_buffer": true,
        "repetition_penalty": 1.0,
        "temperature": 1.0,
        "top_k": 1,
        "top_p": 1.0
    }
}

Next step, let’s look at the hardware I used for this demo.

GPU hardware

My machine has an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell Generation Laptop GPU:

It has 16 GB of VRAM — enough headroom for small models like Phi-3-Mini-4K-Instruct-onnx. Great, right?

Environment

To run this ONNX model on GPU with CUDA, you need four layers of software on top of the hardware:

  • NVIDIA driver — required for any GPU workload; nothing special to add here.
  • CUDA Toolkit — the CUDA SDK (compiler, runtime, debugger, and related tools). Pick a toolkit version that matches your GPU generation. On my Blackwell laptop I use CUDA 13.4. Installing the toolkit takes time, so confirm your GPU architecture and the ORT/GenAI package requirements before you install.
  • cuDNN — NVIDIA’s deep learning primitives library; ONNX Runtime GPU depends on it.
  • Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntimeGenAI.Cuda — the .NET package for CUDA. It pulls in native dependencies such as ONNX Runtime GPU. Package version must align with your CUDA stack—for example, 0.16.0 targets the CUDA 13 line.

Setting this up involves trial and error; give yourself some patience. Once everything is in place, we can move to the demo.

Demo

Switching from CPU to GPU does not require rewriting your agent. You mainly change how the model is loaded.

Lower-level API:

using Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntimeGenAI;
string modelPath = @"C:\path\to\cuda-model";
using Config config = new Config(modelPath);
config.ClearProviders();
config.AppendProvider("cuda");
using Model model = new Model(config);

Higher-level API (Microsoft.Extensions.AI):

using Microsoft.Extensions.AI;
using Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntimeGenAI;
string modelPath = @"C:\path\to\cuda-model";
using Config config = new Config(modelPath);
config.ClearProviders();
config.AppendProvider("cuda");
using var client = new OnnxRuntimeGenAIChatClient(config);
ChatResponse response = await client.GetResponseAsync("Hello", new ChatOptions
{
    MaxOutputTokens = 64,
});

The important line is AppendProvider("cuda").

As we mentioned above, the model folder must be the cuda variant (not cpu_and_mobile). The config snippet simply tells ONNX Runtime GenAI to use the CUDA execution provider at runtime.

CPU vs GPU throughput

First, the CPU run:

438 tokens in 25 seconds — about 17 tokens/s.

Then the GPU run:

Same 438 tokens in 3.5 seconds — about 121 tokens/s. That is roughly a 7–8× speedup. Smart design, right? Most of the win comes from moving matmul-heavy work off the CPU and onto the GPU execution provider.

Summary

After reading this post, you should understand:

  • Why the Hugging Face cuda ONNX build pairs with OnnxRuntimeGenAI.Cuda on .NET.
  • The four-layer stack: driver → CUDA Toolkit → cuDNN → GenAI CUDA NuGet — and why versions must match (especially on newer GPUs such as Blackwell).
  • How little code changes when you switch providers: ClearProviders() + AppendProvider("cuda").
  • What kind of speedup to expect on a small quantized Phi-3 model when CPU and GPU are compared fairly.

About the author

I am Chris Bao, a software engineer focused on Azure and AWS AI platforms, with hands-on experience in cloud AI services and agent development.

For training or consulting, reach me at baoqger@gmail.com.
